---
title: HTTP OpenAPI
description: Generate an OpenAPI 3.1 document from explicit shared HTTP route metadata.
---

## What It Is

`@superfunctions/http-openapi` exports `generateOpenApiDocument`, which converts
route inventories into an OpenAPI 3.1 document. It consumes the `getRoutes()`
interface used by the shared HTTP router. The result is a plain object suitable
for serialization, inspection and version control. Generation does not start a
server or make requests to the handlers described by the document.

## When To Use It

Use this package when a library already defines routes with
`@superfunctions/http` and wants its API description to come from the same route
inventory. This is useful for publishing integration documentation, checking API
changes in CI and supplying a schema to another tool. Your application remains
responsible for serving the resulting JSON and for enforcing authentication on
actual requests. Documentation metadata is not an authorization mechanism.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superfunctions/http @superfunctions/http-openapi
```

Install framework adapters separately when mounting the routes in an application.
The generator needs route definitions, so it can also run in a build script
without importing a running Express, Hono or Next.js server.

## Quick Start

This small inventory documents a health endpoint using the actual generator
input contract. The example handler is included in the route definition but is
not executed during document generation.

```ts
import type { Route } from "@superfunctions/http";
import { generateOpenApiDocument } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";

const routes: Route[] = [{
  method: "GET",
  path: "/health",
  handler: async () => Response.json({ ok: true }),
  meta: { openapi: {
    operationId: "health.read",
    responseSchemas: {
      "200": { type: "object", properties: { ok: { type: "boolean" } } },
    },
  } },
}];
const document = generateOpenApiDocument({
  title: "Service API", version: "1.0.0",
  routers: [{ getRoutes: () => routes }],
});
```

## Core Concepts

Only routes with `meta.openapi` participate. Setting `include: false` explicitly
excludes a route. Included routes require `operationId`; missing identifiers
raise `OpenApiGenerationError` with code `OPENAPI_META_INCOMPLETE`. A duplicate
method and normalized path also fails instead of silently replacing an operation.

Paths such as `/records/:id` become `/records/{id}`. Generated path parameters
are required strings. `requestBodySchema` produces a required JSON request body,
and `responseSchemas` maps status codes to JSON response schemas. Without response
schemas the generator supplies a basic 200 success description. Summary,
description and tags are taken from route metadata. Paths, methods, tags and
schema object keys are sorted for stable output.

## Real-World Example

A build step can serialize a supplied route inventory without constructing a
framework application. Keeping this boundary small lets an application compare
the document in CI while its runtime adapter remains independently configured.

```ts
import type { OpenApiRouter } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";
import { generateOpenApiDocument } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";

export function describeApi(routers: OpenApiRouter[]): string {
  return JSON.stringify(generateOpenApiDocument({
    title: "Operations API", version: "2.0.0", routers,
  }), null, 2);
}
```

## Related Packages

[HTTP](/docs/http/http) defines the router and metadata contracts.
[OAuth Router](/docs/authentication/oauth-router) supplies reusable route
inventories. [Admin](/docs/tooling/admin) has its own administration manifest
projection, including operator security configuration, for administration APIs.

## Troubleshooting

An empty paths object usually means the supplied routes have no OpenAPI metadata
or are excluded. Inspect `getRoutes()` before changing the generator. A schema
error should be corrected in route metadata rather than hidden by dropping the
route. This generator does not infer arbitrary handler types, query parameters
or security schemes from application code; do not assume generated documentation
proves those runtime behaviors are implemented.

---
title: HTTP OpenAPI
description: Generate an OpenAPI 3.1 document from explicit shared HTTP route metadata.
---

## What It Is

`@superfunctions/http-openapi` exports `generateOpenApiDocument`, which converts
route inventories into an OpenAPI 3.1 document. It consumes the `getRoutes()`
interface used by the shared HTTP router. The result is a plain object suitable
for serialization, inspection and version control. Generation does not start a
server or make requests to the handlers described by the document.

## When To Use It

Use this package when a library already defines routes with
`@superfunctions/http` and wants its API description to come from the same route
inventory. This is useful for publishing integration documentation, checking API
changes in CI and supplying a schema to another tool. Your application remains
responsible for serving the resulting JSON and for enforcing authentication on
actual requests. Documentation metadata is not an authorization mechanism.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superfunctions/http @superfunctions/http-openapi
```

Install framework adapters separately when mounting the routes in an application.
The generator needs route definitions, so it can also run in a build script
without importing a running Express, Hono or Next.js server.

## Quick Start

This small inventory documents a health endpoint using the actual generator
input contract. The example handler is included in the route definition but is
not executed during document generation.

```ts
import type { Route } from "@superfunctions/http";
import { generateOpenApiDocument } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";

const routes: Route[] = [{
  method: "GET",
  path: "/health",
  handler: async () => Response.json({ ok: true }),
  meta: { openapi: {
    operationId: "health.read",
    responseSchemas: {
      "200": { type: "object", properties: { ok: { type: "boolean" } } },
    },
  } },
}];
const document = generateOpenApiDocument({
  title: "Service API", version: "1.0.0",
  routers: [{ getRoutes: () => routes }],
});
```

## Core Concepts

Only routes with `meta.openapi` participate. Setting `include: false` explicitly
excludes a route. Included routes require `operationId`; missing identifiers
raise `OpenApiGenerationError` with code `OPENAPI_META_INCOMPLETE`. A duplicate
method and normalized path also fails instead of silently replacing an operation.

Paths such as `/records/:id` become `/records/{id}`. Generated path parameters
are required strings. `requestBodySchema` produces a required JSON request body,
and `responseSchemas` maps status codes to JSON response schemas. Without response
schemas the generator supplies a basic 200 success description. Summary,
description and tags are taken from route metadata. Paths, methods, tags and
schema object keys are sorted for stable output.

## Real-World Example

A build step can serialize a supplied route inventory without constructing a
framework application. Keeping this boundary small lets an application compare
the document in CI while its runtime adapter remains independently configured.

```ts
import type { OpenApiRouter } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";
import { generateOpenApiDocument } from "@superfunctions/http-openapi";

export function describeApi(routers: OpenApiRouter[]): string {
  return JSON.stringify(generateOpenApiDocument({
    title: "Operations API", version: "2.0.0", routers,
  }), null, 2);
}
```

## Related Packages

[HTTP](/docs/http/http) defines the router and metadata contracts.
[OAuth Router](/docs/authentication/oauth-router) supplies reusable route
inventories. [Admin](/docs/tooling/admin) has its own administration manifest
projection, including operator security configuration, for administration APIs.

## Troubleshooting

An empty paths object usually means the supplied routes have no OpenAPI metadata
or are excluded. Inspect `getRoutes()` before changing the generator. A schema
error should be corrected in route metadata rather than hidden by dropping the
route. This generator does not infer arbitrary handler types, query parameters
or security schemes from application code; do not assume generated documentation
proves those runtime behaviors are implemented.

---
title: Observability
description: Shared request observations, structured events, metrics and spans with injected destinations.
---

## What It Is

`@superfunctions/observability` provides a common observation interface for
Superfunctions libraries and applications. It groups request measurements,
structured events and timed spans behind one configurable object. Applications
choose the event and metric destinations and may supply a logger. The package
coordinates these interfaces; it does not provision a monitoring backend or
persist observations in a database by itself.

## When To Use It

Use this package when reusable modules should emit consistent measurements while
remaining independent of the application's telemetry vendor. A storage adapter,
HTTP handler and delivery integration can share service labels and request
identity without importing each other's monitoring clients. It is also useful
for local tests that collect measurements in memory and inspect the resulting
request snapshot. Choose the actual collection, retention and export system at
the application boundary.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superfunctions/observability
```

The default Node request context uses AsyncLocalStorage. Non-Node environments
have a synchronous fallback; applications needing context across asynchronous
boundaries in those environments must inject a `requestContext` implementation.
Do not assume browser and Node propagation behavior are interchangeable.

## Quick Start

Create an observation object with explicit service identity and a metric sink.
This example records measurements in an application-owned array so the behavior
can be inspected without making a network call or claiming durable retention.

```ts
import { createObservability } from "@superfunctions/observability";
import type { ObservationMetric } from "@superfunctions/observability";

const recorded: ObservationMetric[] = [];
const observations = createObservability({
  service: "orders", component: "checkout",
  metrics: metric => { recorded.push(metric); },
});
observations.record({
  kind: "database", operation: "orders.find", durationMs: 12, ok: true,
});
```

## Core Concepts

A metric describes a kind and operation, with optional duration, success flag,
component, resource and labels. An event uses a domain and type plus optional
severity, identities, outcome and metadata. A span measures an operation until
its `end` method is called. These are contracts for application observations,
not an automatic tracing system that instruments every library call.

`startRequest` creates a request observation. `runWithRequest` makes that
observation current while the supplied work executes, using the configured
context implementation. Request snapshots include identity, status, total
duration, grouped measurements and the recorded metrics. Child observation
objects let a subsystem add scope information while sharing the configured
channels. `normalizeObservability` accepts existing observation objects, logger
inputs, configuration objects or disabled values at a library boundary.

## Real-World Example

A request wrapper can explicitly bind a unit of work to request context and
produce a final snapshot. The application decides where that snapshot belongs,
such as a structured completion event or a local diagnostic result.

```ts
import { createObservability } from "@superfunctions/observability";

const telemetry = createObservability({ service: "orders" });
export async function measureRequest(work: () => Promise<void>) {
  const request = telemetry.startRequest({ method: "POST", path: "/orders" });
  await telemetry.runWithRequest(request, async () => {
    const span = telemetry.span({ kind: "application", operation: "orders.create" });
    try { await work(); span.end({ ok: true }); }
    catch (error) { span.end({ ok: false }); throw error; }
  });
  return request.finish({ status: 201 });
}
```

## Related Packages

[Metrics](/docs/middleware-runtime/metrics) provides additional shared metric
primitives. [HTTP](/docs/http/http) supplies request and route contracts.
[Delivery](/docs/middleware-runtime/delivery) describes messaging provider
boundaries that can emit observations through an application-owned channel.

## Troubleshooting

If measurements are missing from your backend, confirm that channels are actually
configured and inspect their transport separately. A local snapshot does not
prove successful export. If request identity disappears after an await in a
non-Node runtime, supply an asynchronous context implementation instead of relying
on the synchronous fallback. Keep label cardinality controlled and redact event
metadata at the application boundary; the observation contract does not make
arbitrary business data safe to export.
EOF

---
title: Admin
description: Function-owned administration manifests, policy-aware dispatch and typed operator clients.
---

## What It Is

`@superfunctions/admin` defines shared administration contracts for Super Console
and self-hosted API consumers. A function describes its resources and operations
in a capability manifest and binds those operations to its domain service. The
same definitions support operator discovery, REST/OpenAPI descriptions, typed
client calls and MCP projection. The package keeps these surfaces aligned without
moving domain behavior into the console or a generic route handler.

## When To Use It

Use this package when a function needs a consistent operator API with explicit
scope, permissions, mutation controls and audit behavior. A deployment can enable
only selected function modules, so installing a package does not automatically
expose its administrative operations. It is also useful when an application
needs typed access to an existing administration deployment. It does not supply
operator identities, a durable audit backend or a domain service automatically.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superfunctions/admin
```

Function-specific client wrappers may require this package as a peer dependency.
Keep the shared client installed in the consuming application so wrappers use the
same public types and runtime instance. Install HTTP or authentication adapters
separately according to the deployment's request and identity boundaries.

## Quick Start

Registry enablement is explicit. An empty registry is a useful starting point
for an installation that must expose no function administration until adapters
and an allowlist are supplied by deployment configuration.

```ts
import { createAdminRegistry } from "@superfunctions/admin";

const registry = createAdminRegistry({
  adapters: [],
  enabledModules: [],
});
```

A function author uses `defineAdminCapability` to define the manifest and
`createAdminCapabilityAdapter` to bind operation IDs to implementations. Add those
adapters to the registry and enable their module IDs deliberately. An unavailable
capability cannot become operational merely by adding its ID to the allowlist.

## Core Concepts

Manifests describe resources, operation input and output schemas, permissions,
HTTP routes, safety classifications and optional presentation metadata. The
registry validates dependencies and rejects collisions. Presentation describes
operator controls but does not change authorization or mutation safety. The
dispatcher repeats the relevant policy checks when an operation is invoked.

Scopes follow installation, workspace, project and environment hierarchy. An
operation requiring a deeper scope needs the complete chain. Mutations declare
required audit, and destructive operations require confirmation. Idempotency
identities bind the request key to actor, scope and operation, preventing a key
from silently authorizing a different operation or payload.

Memory audit and idempotency implementations are suitable for development and
tests. Production deployments need durable implementations with the documented
atomic claim, fencing and audit reconciliation semantics. Audit and domain
storage are separate transactions; monitoring must account for an attempted
operation whose terminal audit outcome is not yet confirmed.

## Real-World Example

An application can use the shared client to discover enabled capabilities at a
particular tenant scope. Authentication remains part of the deployment's
transport configuration; the scope object is not an authentication credential.

```ts
import { createAdminClient } from "@superfunctions/admin";

export async function inspectAdministration(baseUrl: string) {
  const client = createAdminClient({
    baseUrl,
    scope: {
      installationId: "install_1", workspaceId: "workspace_1",
      projectId: "project_1",
    },
    timeoutMs: 30000,
  });
  return await client.registry();
}
```

## Related Packages

[Auth](/docs/authentication/auth) supplies authentication abstractions.
[HTTP](/docs/http/http) supplies shared request and router contracts.
[HTTP OpenAPI](/docs/http/http-openapi) generates descriptions from general HTTP
routes; administration manifests have their own projection through
`createAdminOpenApiDocument` with deployment-specific security configuration.

## Troubleshooting

A missing navigation entry or operation may mean its module is disabled, lacks
an implementation or is filtered by discovery policy. Check the registry and
scope before adding custom routes around the dispatcher. For mutation failures,
inspect the confirmation, idempotency and audit requirements rather than retrying
with a new key immediately. An uncertain domain outcome must remain fenced until
reconciled; bypassing that boundary can repeat a destructive side effect.

A function author uses `defineAdminCapability` to define the manifest and
`createAdminCapabilityAdapter` to bind operation IDs to implementations. Add those
adapters to the registry and enable their module IDs deliberately. An unavailable
capability cannot become operational merely by adding its ID to the allowlist.

## Core Concepts

Manifests describe resources, operation input and output schemas, permissions,
HTTP routes, safety classifications and optional presentation metadata. The
registry validates dependencies and rejects collisions. Presentation describes
operator controls but does not change authorization or mutation safety. The
dispatcher repeats the relevant policy checks when an operation is invoked.

Scopes follow installation, workspace, project and environment hierarchy. An
operation requiring a deeper scope needs the complete chain. Mutations declare
required audit, and destructive operations require confirmation. Idempotency
identities bind the request key to actor, scope and operation, preventing a key
from silently authorizing a different operation or payload.

Memory audit and idempotency implementations are suitable for development and
tests. Production deployments need durable implementations with the documented
atomic claim, fencing and audit reconciliation semantics. Audit and domain
storage are separate transactions; monitoring must account for an attempted
operation whose terminal audit outcome is not yet confirmed.

## Real-World Example

An application can use the shared client to discover enabled capabilities at a
particular tenant scope. Authentication remains part of the deployment's
transport configuration; the scope object is not an authentication credential.

```ts
import { createAdminClient } from "@superfunctions/admin";

export async function inspectAdministration(baseUrl: string) {
  const client = createAdminClient({
    baseUrl,
    scope: {
      installationId: "install_1", workspaceId: "workspace_1",
      projectId: "project_1",
    },
    timeoutMs: 30000,
  });
  return await client.registry();
}
```

## Related Packages

[Auth](/docs/authentication/auth) supplies authentication abstractions.
[HTTP](/docs/http/http) supplies shared request and router contracts.
[HTTP OpenAPI](/docs/http/http-openapi) generates descriptions from general HTTP
routes; administration manifests have their own projection through
`createAdminOpenApiDocument` with deployment-specific security configuration.

## Troubleshooting

A missing navigation entry or operation may mean its module is disabled, lacks
an implementation or is filtered by discovery policy. Check the registry and
scope before adding custom routes around the dispatcher. For mutation failures,
inspect the confirmation, idempotency and audit requirements rather than retrying
with a new key immediately. An uncertain domain outcome must remain fenced until
reconciled; bypassing that boundary can repeat a destructive side effect.

title: OAuth Router
description: Expose reusable OAuth routes with secure defaults on top of the shared oauth-flow service.
---

`@superfunctions/oauth-router` turns `oauth-flow` into a reusable route inventory instead of forcing every app to hand-write the same start, callback, and disconnect handlers. It is intentionally small: route factories in, framework adapters out. Your app still chooses the HTTP adapter, auth/session boundary, and how request context becomes flow input.

## What It Is

The package exports two route factories:

- `createOAuthBrowserRoutes(...)`
- `createOAuthConnectionRoutes(...)`

Both return `@superfunctions/http` `Route[]` definitions that can be mounted through any supported HTTP adapter.

## When To Use It

Use `oauth-router` when you already want `oauth-flow` but also want consistent route exposure across apps:

- browser auth / social-login style flows
- customer connection management routes
- packages such as `plugfn` that should not duplicate HTTP handler glue in every integration surface

If your app needs completely custom routing, you can still call `flowService.start()`, `handleCallback()`, and `disconnect()` directly.

## Install

```bash
npm install @superfunctions/oauth-router @superfunctions/oauth-flow @superfunctions/http
```

Use your preferred HTTP adapter in the app layer, for example `@superfunctions/http-express` or `@superfunctions/http-hono`.

## Quick Start

```ts
import { createOAuthBrowserRoutes } from "@superfunctions/oauth-router";
import type { OAuthBrowserRouteConfig } from "@superfunctions/oauth-router";

export function browserRoutes(
  flowService: OAuthBrowserRouteConfig["flowService"],
  resolveStartInput: OAuthBrowserRouteConfig["resolveStartInput"],
) {
  return createOAuthBrowserRoutes({
    basePath: "/auth/social", flowService, resolveStartInput,
    callbackMode: "json",
  });
}
```

## Core Concepts

Each factory returns three routes under its base path: `POST /start`,
`GET /callback/:provider`, and `POST /disconnect/:provider`. The start resolver
converts the application request into an `OAuthFlowStartInput`. Keep tenant,
actor and permitted-provider decisions in trusted application code rather than
copying an arbitrary request body into that input. The default request ID header
is `x-request-id`; `requestIdHeader` changes that lookup.

Authentication modes are route metadata. Their enforcement still depends on the
application middleware and adapter configuration. Declaring a mode does not
create a session resolver or establish a logged-in user by itself.

### Default Route Posture

The factories now ship with secure defaults:

- browser routes: `start=none`, `callback=none`, `disconnect=hybrid`
- connection routes: `start=hybrid`, `callback=none`, `disconnect=hybrid`

That keeps provider callbacks open while avoiding unauthenticated disconnect by default.

## Real-World Example

A connection-management API can require a bearer scope on its start route while
leaving provider callbacks reachable. Supply the resolver from your application
after validating the signed-in actor and permitted connection destination. This
example exposes that dependency explicitly; it does not trust client-provided
identity fields.

### Route Metadata Overrides

You can override metadata per route through `routeMeta`, and overrides merge shallowly with nested `auth` and `openapi` objects.

```ts
import { createOAuthConnectionRoutes } from "@superfunctions/oauth-router";
import type { OAuthConnectionRouteConfig } from "@superfunctions/oauth-router";

export function connectionRoutes(
  flowService: OAuthConnectionRouteConfig["flowService"],
  resolveStartInput: OAuthConnectionRouteConfig["resolveStartInput"],
) {
return createOAuthConnectionRoutes({
  basePath: "/oauth/connections",
  flowService,
  resolveStartInput,
  routeMeta: {
    start: {
      auth: {
        mode: "bearer",
        scopes: ["connections:write"],
      },
    },
  },
});
}
```

## Related Packages

- [`oauth-flow`](/docs/authentication/oauth-flow) owns lifecycle orchestration.
- [`oauth-router`](/docs/authentication/oauth-router) owns reusable route definitions.
- `@superfunctions/http-*` adapters own framework-specific mounting.

That split is what lets apps such as `plugfn` reuse one lifecycle engine and one route inventory across Express, Hono, Fastify, or other adapters without copying auth metadata and callback parsing logic into every app.

## Troubleshooting

If callback routes fail because a request is blocked before it reaches `oauth-flow`, inspect your adapter/session middleware before blaming the provider. If a route needs stricter auth metadata than the defaults, use `routeMeta` instead of cloning the factory. If your app needs redirect-on-callback behavior for browser auth, use the browser route factory’s callback mode options rather than building a parallel custom callback stack.

Browser callbacks can return JSON or redirect, with a callback-mode function
selecting the behavior per result. Redirect locations are checked against the
request origin and explicitly configured `allowedRedirectOrigins`; the factory
rejects invalid redirect targets. Configure full trusted origins, and keep
provider callback URLs consistent with the flow service configuration. Result
serialization can be customized with `serializeCallbackResult`, which is useful
when the UI needs a small response instead of the full flow result.

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)


### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```

```

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)

# Router destination enforcement checkpoint — 2026-10-22

Requirement: SEC-001, original audit-fix SPEC Security 1–2 and Limits 5.
This checkpoint closes the reproduced default `/web/page` loopback request and
caller-controlled image private-host override. It does not establish full
production readiness or complete SEC-001.

## Behavior

- Both routers overwrite page/metadata security with `allowPrivateHosts: false`
  and disable cache. Metadata propagates the mandatory option to each page fetch.
  Image download routers overwrite the legacy `allowPrivateHosts` flag; the
  TypeScript router also prevents a custom provider download from bypassing it.
- Static page HTTP(S) transport checks literal addresses and every DNS answer,
  rejects mixed public/private answer sets, and uses the checked address directly.
  Node supplies checked answers through the socket lookup; Python connects to the
  checked IP with the original Host and TLS SNI identity. No proxy/environment
  proxy is used. TLS certificate verification remains enabled.
- Every redirect repeats the policy, including scheme/credential checks; five
  redirects maximum. Caller headers are dropped on origin changes.
- Bodies are capped at 10 MiB by declared length and cumulative bytes; identity
  encoding is requested and compressed responses are rejected. The overall
  deadline covers DNS, headers, redirect chain and body, with UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT.
- Policy errors are terminal for fallback and retry. Before invocation or
  availability probing, protected web calls reject browser, hosted and custom
  providers that lack the transport boundary. Python protected cookies and all
  protected proxies are rejected. No browser is launched by a rejected call.
- Direct library calls can explicitly select protected static transport or opt
  into private hosts. Legacy calls omitting security retain existing behavior;
  they must not be exposed to untrusted URLs. Protected direct callers must
  disable cache themselves; HTTP callers cannot override that setting.

## Evidence

Committed TypeScript and Python tests use owned ephemeral HTTP servers. Actual
router calls deny loopback (including Node URL numeric/hex normalization) without
any target request despite body security/cache overrides. Metadata reports item
failure, and image override denial also receives no target request. Explicit
private-host opt-in fetches and follows a relative redirect, preserving final URL
metadata. Custom fallback is never invoked after a policy denial.

DNS fixtures inject a mixed public/private response and observe zero connections;
positive checked-address fixtures assert the hostname is resolved once. Redirect
fixtures classify only the owned origin as public for the test, leaving the
private redirect destination denied and unrequested. This is deterministic local
evidence, not a claim of a public production network experiment. No external
host was probed. TypeScript also exercises chunked payload overflow; both
languages cover declared overflow, redirect loops, invalid redirect scheme,
compressed-response rejection and timeout.

Validation:

- TypeScript full suite: 139 passing, including 9 destination-policy tests.
  SDK/admin typechecks and builds pass.
- Python fresh 3.12 environment: 101 passing, including 7 destination-policy
  tests. Earlier system 3.9 focused
  service/router/provider/middleware run: 30 passing.
- System 3.9 full collection lacked Pillow; fresh 3.12 resolves the required
  dependencies. Test-extra installation required local shared python-core and
  python-sqlalchemy 0.1.1 because the published sqlalchemy adapter is 0.1.0.
  No dependency manifests or shared source were changed.

Logs: `/tmp/browse-policy-{tests,all,types,build,python,python-all,python-focused,install}.log`.

## Outstanding original requirements

Browser functionality under a real egress boundary remains required. Request
interception or preflight DNS alone cannot certify browser subresources,
WebSockets, service workers, WebRTC/QUIC and DNS rebinding. A pinned HTTP/CONNECT
proxy is a possible component, but must be paired with process/network isolation
preventing alternate egress and verified for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
Existing browser providers have no such sandbox; they are rejected here rather
than represented as safe. Remote hosted providers need separately established
remote egress guarantees. Custom provider support, exact allowedHosts policy,
default direct-library migration, bounded compressed response decoding and
cookie forwarding remain unfinished. Private networking via a globally routed
address or unusual deployment routing also requires deployment firewall policy.
No browser sandbox, deployment, TLS certificate fixture, external service
integration, hosted CI result, or full secret-redaction audit is claimed by these
local transport tests.

# ContentFn response validation and server type safety

2026-10-22 UTC. Follow-up to release authorization checkpoint `cc6e4f81e`.

## Correctness and contract

CmsFn's seven ContentFn clients now share a local typed transport-envelope validator. ContentFn business failures commonly arrive as HTTP 200 `{ ok: false, error }` responses. Previously the audit clients converted those failures into successful empty lists, while other clients returned unchecked shapes and non-CmsFn error codes. Malformed JSON, malformed envelopes/results, network failures and non-success HTTP responses containing success envelopes now return errors. Neither a missing result nor a broken upstream service is an empty successful audit page.

The validator checks the literal boolean discriminant and error code/message/details types. Known shared codes retain their identity. ContentFn missing-resource codes map to `NOT_FOUND`; existing-resource/revision-conflict codes map to `CONFLICT`; schema/patch/query validation codes map to `VALIDATION_FAILED`. Other foreign codes map to `CONTENTFN_UNAVAILABLE`. Mapped and unknown original codes remain in `error.details.upstreamCode`; HTTP status remains in `upstreamStatus`. These fields override similarly named upstream detail fields. Parser/network error messages do not include response bodies or exception text. Valid upstream error messages and other error details remain visible as before.

Endpoint-specific consumers validate the fields they use:

- Draft and published documents must match the requested identity and contain a string type; optional revision and workflow-state fields must have the expected shapes. Other document fields remain opaque JSON. CmsFn uses a small validated local HTTP projection instead of an undeclared `@contentfn/core` package import.
- Export requires format version 1, the requested dataset, a string export time, schema presence and the four array sections. Their contents remain opaque; this is not ContentFn's full archive/schema validator. Import and unpublish require their documented empty-object result.
- Audit pages require arrays and a string-or-null cursor. Events and deliveries must match the requested dataset. Events project only documented document identifiers, actor subject and changed paths; arbitrary nested body/secret fields are omitted. Invalid nested shapes and delivery statuses/attempts fail the page instead of manufacturing defaults.

The source contract was inspected in ContentFn core errors, HTTP router, docs/publish endpoints and storage, and import/export format/endpoints at sibling source head `842eb1b7e9bcb108d575af318249b256b63f8e48`. That router does **not** provide `/contentfn/audit/events` or `/contentfn/audit/webhooks`. This change does not invent those producer endpoints or claim functional audit integration.

## Type safety

Full `@cmsfn/server` typecheck now passes, replacing the 143 historical diagnostics recorded at the preceding checkpoint. No compiler options, shared packages, dependencies or lockfiles changed. Production unknown response values are narrowed at runtime. Existing HTTP tests now use an envelope reader and checked field/array/string helpers that keep result data unknown until inspected; their assertions remain intact. The remaining narrow source corrections widen the status capability accumulator to strings and accept structured objects directly in the existing logger filter instead of casting them to an index-signature type.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: passes.
- `npm test --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: 87 tests pass in 13 files.
- `npm run build --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: ESM, CJS and declaration outputs pass.
- Nine new transport tests use owned real HTTP servers across all seven clients: success and result projection, malformed JSON/envelopes/results, HTTP 500 success contradictions, HTTP 200/403 business failures, unknown-code preservation, foreign-code mapping, closed connections, mismatched document identity, unsafe audit nested fields and wrong datasets.
- Built CmsFn and the existing built ContentFn sibling were served together on owned local HTTP sockets with memory adapters. Dataset export succeeded. Missing dataset export and missing document release publication mapped actual ContentFn codes to `NOT_FOUND`. Both unsupported audit routes returned error envelopes with upstream status 404, confirming the integration gap remains visible. All servers were closed. This is local producer/consumer evidence, not deployment evidence.

Logs: `/tmp/cms-transport-types.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-tests.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-build.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-producer-http.log`.

## Remaining scope

Other route authorization and request limits, upstream authentication forwarding/configuration, response byte/time limits, complete producer audit APIs, full export archive validation, release scheduling, concurrent mutations, database-provider acceptance and studio workflows remain separate requirements. Network requests are not retried; errors do not prove an attempted upstream mutation was rolled back. Passing full server typecheck does not establish whole-function production readiness.

{"chunk_id":"5133a0","wall_time_seconds":0.000007292,"exit_code":1,"original_token_count":1650,"output":"# ContentFn response validation and server type safety

2026-10-22 UTC. Follow-up to release authorization checkpoint `cc6e4f81e`.

## Correctness and contract

CmsFn's seven ContentFn clients now share a local typed transport-envelope validator. ContentFn business failures commonly arrive as HTTP 200 `{ ok: false, error }` responses. Previously the audit clients converted those failures into successful empty lists, while other clients returned unchecked shapes and non-CmsFn error codes. Malformed JSON, malformed envelopes/results, network failures and non-success HTTP responses containing success envelopes now return errors. Neither a missing result nor a broken upstream service is an empty successful audit page.

The validator checks the literal boolean discriminant and error code/message/details types. Known shared codes retain their identity. ContentFn missing-resource codes map to `NOT_FOUND`; existing-resource/revision-conflict codes map to `CONFLICT`; schema/patch/query validation codes map to `VALIDATION_FAILED`. Other foreign codes map to `CONTENTFN_UNAVAILABLE`. Mapped and unknown original codes remain in `error.details.upstreamCode`; HTTP status remains in `upstreamStatus`. These fields override similarly named upstream detail fields. Parser/network error messages do not include response bodies or exception text. Valid upstream error messages and other error details remain visible as before.

Endpoint-specific consumers validate the fields they use:

- Draft and published documents must match the requested identity and contain a string type; optional revision and workflow-state fields must have the expected shapes. Other document fields remain opaque JSON. CmsFn uses a small validated local HTTP projection instead of an undeclared `@contentfn/core` package import.
- Export requires format version 1, the requested dataset, a string export time, schema presence and the four array sections. Their contents remain opaque; this is not ContentFn's full archive/schema validator. Import and unpublish require their documented empty-object result.
- Audit pages require arrays and a string-or-null cursor. Events and deliveries must match the requested dataset. Events project only documented document identifiers, actor subject and changed paths; arbitrary nested body/secret fields are omitted. Invalid nested shapes and delivery statuses/attempts fail the page instead of manufacturing defaults.

The source contract was inspected in ContentFn core errors, HTTP router, docs/publish endpoints and storage, and import/export format/endpoints at sibling source head `842eb1b7e9bcb108d575af318249b256b63f8e48`. That router does **not** provide `/contentfn/audit/events` or `/contentfn/audit/webhooks`. This change does not invent those producer endpoints or claim functional audit integration.

## Type safety

Full `@cmsfn/server` typecheck now passes, replacing the 143 historical diagnostics recorded at the preceding checkpoint. No compiler options, shared packages, dependencies or lockfiles changed. Production unknown response values are narrowed at runtime. Existing HTTP tests now use an envelope reader and checked field/array/string helpers that keep result data unknown until inspected; their assertions remain intact. The remaining narrow source corrections widen the status capability accumulator to strings and accept structured objects directly in the existing logger filter instead of casting them to an index-signature type.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: passes.
- `npm test --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: 87 tests pass in 13 files.
- `npm run build --workspace=@cmsfn/server`: ESM, CJS and declaration outputs pass.
- Nine new transport tests use owned real HTTP servers across all seven clients: success and result projection, malformed JSON/envelopes/results, HTTP 500 success contradictions, HTTP 200/403 business failures, unknown-code preservation, foreign-code mapping, closed connections, mismatched document identity, unsafe audit nested fields and wrong datasets.
- Built CmsFn and the existing built ContentFn sibling were served together on owned local HTTP sockets with memory adapters. Dataset export succeeded. Missing dataset export and missing document release publication mapped actual ContentFn codes to `NOT_FOUND`. Both unsupported audit routes returned error envelopes with upstream status 404, confirming the integration gap remains visible. All servers were closed. This is local producer/consumer evidence, not deployment evidence.

Logs: `/tmp/cms-transport-types.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-tests.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-build.log`, `/tmp/cms-transport-producer-http.log`.

## Remaining scope

Other route authorization and request limits, upstream authentication forwarding/configuration, response byte/time limits, complete producer audit APIs, full export archive validation, release scheduling, concurrent mutations, database-provider acceptance and studio workflows remain separate requirements. Network requests are not retried; errors do not prove an attempted upstream mutation was rolled back. Passing full server typecheck does not establish whole-function production readiness.
